title: Police are not registering my complaint (FIR)
summary: If you report a cognizable offence (such as theft, assault, cheating or threats), the police must register an FIR. Here is how to escalate if they refuse.
urgent: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 112 first.

steps.title: Write down what happened
steps.detail: Write a short, dated complaint stating who, what, when, where and how, with names of witnesses and any proof. Keep a copy.
steps.why: A written complaint creates a record that cannot later be denied.

steps.title: Submit it at the police station and ask for an FIR
steps.detail: Hand the complaint to the Station House Officer (SHO). You may file at any police station; a Zero FIR must be registered even if the incident happened elsewhere. Ask for a free copy of the FIR.
steps.why: BNSS Section 173 makes registration mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence.

steps.title: Get a receipt if the FIR is not registered
steps.detail: If they refuse, ask them to stamp and sign a receiving copy of your complaint, or send it by registered post or email to the SHO. Note the officer's name and the time.
steps.why: Proof that you approached the police is needed for the next steps.

steps.title: Try e-FIR or the state police portal
steps.detail: Many states allow online FIRs (e-FIR) for certain offences such as theft. Cyber offences can be reported at cybercrime.gov.in.
steps.why: An electronic complaint must be signed within three days and is then registered as an FIR.

steps.title: Send the complaint to the Superintendent of Police
steps.detail: Send the substance of your complaint in writing, by registered post, to the SP or DCP of the district, enclosing proof that the station refused.
steps.why: Under BNSS Section 173(4) the SP must investigate or direct an investigation.

steps.title: Apply to the Magistrate
steps.detail: If the SP also does not act, file an application with an affidavit before the Judicial Magistrate asking the court to direct the police to register the FIR and investigate. You may also file a private complaint.
steps.why: BNSS Section 175(3) empowers the Magistrate to order an investigation.

steps.title: Complain about the officer
steps.detail: You can also complain to the State or District Police Complaints Authority or the State Human Rights Commission about the officer's refusal.
steps.why: Officers who fail to register FIRs can face departmental action (Lalita Kumari).

dos: Keep copies of everything you submit
Get the name and rank of the officer you met
Stay calm and polite but firm
Take a friend or relative with you
donts: Do not sign a statement you have not read or that is wrong
Do not accept a 'settlement' under pressure
Do not pay any money to get an FIR registered

rights.right: Registration of an FIR is mandatory for a cognizable offence
rights.source: BNSS Section 173; Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.

rights.right: You can file a Zero FIR at any police station
A free copy of the FIR must be given to you
Escalate to the SP, then the Magistrate, if refused
You must be told the progress of the investigation within 90 days

documents: Evidence: photos, videos, messages, medical report, bills

authorities.name: Superintendent of Police / DCP
authorities.role: Acts on written complaint under BNSS 173(4)

authorities.name: Police Complaints Authority / State Human Rights Commission

title: Police arrest or detention
summary: Whether you, a family member or a friend has been picked up by the police, these rights apply from the moment of arrest.
urgent: Contact a lawyer or your District Legal Services Authority (15100) immediately; free legal aid is available to persons in custody.

steps.title: Ask why and under which section
steps.detail: Ask the officer for the grounds of arrest and the offence. Note the officer's name, rank and police station.
steps.why: You have a right to know the grounds of arrest (BNSS Section 47, Article 22).

steps.title: Check the arrest memo
steps.detail: An arrest memo must be prepared with the date and time, attested by a witness (family member or local person) and signed by the arrested person.
steps.why: Required by D.K. Basu guidelines, now in BNSS Section 36.

steps.title: Make sure family is informed
steps.detail: The police must inform a relative or friend about the arrest and where the person is held.
steps.why: BNSS Section 48.

steps.title: Ask whether the offence is bailable
steps.detail: For a bailable offence, the person has the right to be released on bail by the police station itself on furnishing bail.
steps.why: BNSS Sections 47(2) and 478.

steps.title: Contact a lawyer
steps.detail: The arrested person may meet a lawyer during interrogation. If you cannot afford one, contact the DLSA legal aid clinic or the remand advocate at court.
steps.why: BNSS Section 38 and Article 22(1); free legal aid under the LSA Act.

steps.title: Ensure production before a Magistrate within 24 hours
steps.detail: The person must be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time). Apply for bail at that hearing.
steps.why: Article 22(2) and BNSS Section 58.

steps.title: Report injuries or torture
steps.detail: Ask for a medical examination and tell the Magistrate about any ill-treatment. Request preservation of CCTV footage.
steps.why: BNSS Section 53; Paramvir Singh Saini directions on CCTV.

steps.title: If arrest is feared, consider anticipatory bail
steps.detail: If you fear arrest in a non-bailable case, a lawyer can apply to the Sessions Court or High Court for anticipatory bail.
steps.why: BNSS Section 482.

dos: Stay calm and do not resist
Remember the officer's details
Keep the FIR number and police station name
Tell the Magistrate about any mistreatment
donts: Do not sign blank papers
Do not make a confession to the police; it is not admissible and you cannot be forced to self-incriminate
Do not pay bribes

rights.right: To know the grounds of arrest
To have a relative or friend informed
To meet a lawyer during interrogation
To be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours
To medical examination
Women may not be arrested after sunset and before sunrise except in exceptional cases with a Magistrate's permission
To remain silent and not be forced to be a witness against yourself
To free legal aid
rights.source: Article 39A; Legal Services Authorities Act Section 12

documents: FIR copy (also check the state police website)
Identity and address proof for bail
Surety's identity and property or income documents

authorities.name: Judicial Magistrate
authorities.role: Hears remand and bail; record complaints of ill-treatment

authorities.name: District Legal Services Authority (DLSA)
authorities.role: Free lawyer for persons in custody

title: Domestic violence or dowry harassment
summary: Physical, sexual, emotional or economic abuse by a husband, partner or in-laws is domestic violence. You can get protection, the right to stay in your home, and financial support.
urgent: If you are in danger now, call 112 or the Women Helpline 181. Go to a safe place first.

steps.title: Get to safety
steps.detail: If you are hurt or threatened, call 112 or 181. Go to a trusted relative, friend or a One Stop Centre (Sakhi Centre), which offers shelter, medical help and legal help under one roof.
steps.why: Your safety comes before paperwork.

steps.title: Get medical treatment and a record
steps.detail: Visit a government hospital for any injury and ask for a medico-legal report (MLC).
steps.why: Medical records are strong evidence of physical abuse.

steps.title: Preserve evidence
steps.detail: Keep photos of injuries, threatening messages, call recordings, dowry demand messages, bank records and a diary of incidents with dates.
steps.why: Courts rely on a consistent record of incidents.

steps.title: Contact the Protection Officer
steps.detail: Each district has a Protection Officer who will record a Domestic Incident Report (DIR), help you apply to the Magistrate, and arrange shelter, medical help and legal aid.
steps.why: PWDVA Sections 8 and 9.

steps.title: Apply to the Magistrate under Section 12
steps.detail: File an application for protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, custody of children and compensation. You can ask for urgent interim orders.
steps.why: PWDVA Sections 12 and 18 to 23.

steps.title: File a police complaint if there is cruelty or a dowry demand
steps.detail: Cruelty by the husband or relatives (BNS Section 85) and dowry demands (Dowry Prohibition Act Section 4) are criminal offences. You can file an FIR at the women's cell or any police station.
steps.why: Criminal law is a separate remedy from the civil DV Act reliefs; you can use both.

steps.title: Claim maintenance
steps.detail: You can claim maintenance for yourself and your children under the DV Act, BNSS Section 144 or your personal law.
steps.why: Rajnesh v. Neha requires both sides to disclose their income and assets.

steps.title: Get free legal aid
steps.detail: All women are entitled to free legal services. Contact the DLSA or call 15100.
steps.why: Legal Services Authorities Act Section 12.

dos: Keep copies of your ID, marriage certificate, bank and property documents in a safe place
Make a list of your stridhan (jewellery and gifts)
Tell a trusted person about your situation
Save helpline numbers
donts: Do not leave your children behind if you fear for them; seek custody orders
Do not sign any documents giving up rights to your home or stridhan
Do not delete abusive messages

rights.right: To live in the shared household even if you do not own it
rights.source: PWDVA Section 17; Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja

rights.right: To protection orders stopping violence and contact
To monetary relief, maintenance and compensation
To temporary custody of children
To file against female relatives such as the mother-in-law
rights.source: Hiral P. Harsora v. Kusum Harsora

rights.right: To get your stridhan and dowry back
rights.source: Dowry Prohibition Act Section 6; BNS Section 316

rights.right: To free legal aid

documents: Medical reports and photographs of injuries
Messages, emails or recordings of threats or dowry demands
Income and property details of the husband, if known
Children's birth certificates and school records

authorities.name: Protection Officer (District Women and Child Development Office)
authorities.role: Domestic Incident Report, help with application, shelter

authorities.name: One Stop Centre (Sakhi)
authorities.role: Shelter, medical, police and legal help

authorities.name: Police (Women Cell / Mahila Thana)
authorities.role: FIR for cruelty and dowry offences

authorities.name: State Commission for Women / National Commission for Women

title: Sexual harassment at work
summary: Unwelcome sexual remarks, touching, requests for favours or a hostile environment at work is sexual harassment. The POSH Act gives you a complaint process with protection.
urgent: If you face physical assault or threats, you can also call 112 and file a police complaint.

steps.title: Record every incident
steps.detail: Write down dates, times, places, what was said or done, and who saw it. Save emails, chats and messages.
steps.why: A clear timeline strengthens your complaint.

steps.title: Find the Internal Committee (IC/ICC)
steps.detail: Every employer with 10 or more employees must have an Internal Committee. Its members' names should be displayed at the workplace or on the intranet.
steps.why: POSH Act Section 4.

steps.title: File a written complaint within 3 months
steps.detail: Submit a written complaint to the Internal Committee within 3 months of the incident (or the last incident). The Committee can extend this by 3 more months. If there is no IC, or the complaint is against the employer, approach the Local Committee through the District Officer, or use the SHe-Box portal.
steps.why: POSH Act Sections 6 and 9.

steps.title: Ask for interim relief
steps.detail: During the inquiry you may ask to be transferred, for the harasser to be transferred, or for paid leave of up to 3 months.
steps.why: POSH Act Section 12.

steps.title: Take part in the inquiry
steps.detail: The Committee must finish its inquiry within 90 days, giving both sides a hearing. Conciliation happens only if you ask, and cannot involve a monetary settlement.
steps.why: POSH Act Sections 10 and 11.

steps.title: Follow up on action
steps.detail: The employer must act on the Committee's recommendations within 60 days. You can appeal the findings within 90 days.
steps.why: POSH Act Sections 13 and 18.

steps.title: Consider a police complaint as well
steps.detail: Sexual harassment, stalking and outraging modesty are also crimes under BNS Sections 74, 75 and 78. The employer must assist you if you wish to file.
steps.why: POSH Act Section 19(g).

dos: Keep copies of your complaint and all replies
Tell a trusted colleague or friend
Note the names of any witnesses
Ask for the Committee's written report
donts: Do not resign before thinking it through; you are protected from retaliation
Do not delete messages or emails
Do not agree to a money settlement for withdrawing the complaint

rights.right: To a workplace free of sexual harassment
rights.source: POSH Act Section 3; Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan

rights.right: To complain to the Internal or Local Committee
To interim relief (transfer or leave) during the inquiry
To confidentiality of your identity
To compensation from the harasser if the complaint is proved
To file a criminal complaint

documents: Appointment letter or ID card (proof of employment)

authorities.name: Internal Committee (IC/ICC)
authorities.role: Inquiry into complaints at your workplace

authorities.name: Local Committee (through the District Officer)
authorities.role: Complaints where there is no IC or against the employer

title: Salary not paid or wrongful termination
summary: Employers must pay wages on time and full dues within two working days of exit. If you were not paid, or were fired without notice, here is how to claim.

steps.title: Collect proof of employment and dues
steps.detail: Gather your offer or appointment letter, ID card, salary slips, bank statements showing past salary credits, attendance records, and emails or chats about payment.
steps.why: You must show that you worked and how much is owed.

steps.title: Ask in writing
steps.detail: Email HR or the employer asking for the unpaid salary by a specific date. Keep the email.
steps.why: A written request shows the employer was told and refused.

steps.title: Send a legal demand notice
steps.detail: If unpaid, send a legal notice by registered post or email demanding payment within 15 days, failing which you will approach the authorities.
steps.why: Many employers pay at this stage; it also forms part of your record.

steps.title: File a claim with the Labour Department
steps.detail: File a claim before the authority under the Code on Wages (usually the Labour Commissioner or Deputy Labour Commissioner of your district). Central-sphere establishments can be approached through the Samadhan portal.
steps.why: Code on Wages Section 45 provides a quick remedy for wage claims.

steps.title: For termination, raise an industrial dispute
steps.detail: If you are a 'workman' and were dismissed or retrenched without notice or compensation, approach the conciliation officer and then the Labour Court.
steps.why: Industrial Disputes Act Sections 2A and 25F (now the Industrial Relations Code).

steps.title: Consider a civil suit or other remedies
steps.detail: Managerial employees not covered by labour law can file a civil suit for recovery, often after a legal notice. A bounced salary cheque gives a separate remedy under NI Act Section 138.
steps.why: Different laws apply depending on your role and salary.

dos: Keep copies of salary slips and bank statements
Communicate in writing
Note the deadline: claims should be filed as early as possible (generally within three years)
donts: Do not sign a resignation or 'full and final settlement' you disagree with
Do not hand over company property without a written acknowledgement
Do not share your login credentials before you are paid

rights.right: Monthly wages must be paid before the 7th of the next month
Full dues within 2 working days of resignation, dismissal or removal
No deductions beyond those authorised, and never more than 50%
At least the minimum wage and equal pay regardless of gender
Notice and retrenchment compensation for workmen
Gratuity after 5 years of continuous service

title: Defective product, poor service or online shopping problem
summary: If a product is defective, a service is deficient, you were overcharged, or a refund is refused, you can file a consumer complaint without a lawyer.

steps.title: Collect your proof of purchase
steps.detail: Keep the bill or invoice, order confirmation, warranty card, payment proof and photos or videos of the defect.
steps.why: These prove you are a consumer and what went wrong.

steps.title: Complain to the seller or service provider
steps.detail: Raise a complaint through customer care or email and note the ticket number. Give them a reasonable time to fix it.
steps.why: A record of your complaint and their response is useful evidence.

steps.title: Call the National Consumer Helpline
steps.detail: Call 1915 or register a grievance at consumerhelpline.gov.in. Many companies resolve complaints at this pre-litigation stage.
steps.why: It is free and often quick.

steps.title: Send a legal notice
steps.detail: Send a written notice demanding a refund, replacement or compensation within 15 days.
steps.why: It shows you gave the opposite party an opportunity before going to the Commission.

steps.title: File a complaint before the District Commission
steps.detail: File online through the e-Jagriti portal or in person at the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission where you live or work. Claims up to Rs. 50 lakh go to the District Commission. A small fee applies, and none for claims up to Rs. 5 lakh.
steps.why: Consumer Protection Act Sections 34 and 35.

steps.title: Attend hearings or mediation
steps.detail: The Commission may refer the matter to mediation. You can represent yourself.
steps.why: Consumer Protection Act Section 37 and Chapter V.

dos: File within 2 years of the problem
Keep all communication in writing
Claim compensation for mental agony and litigation costs too
donts: Do not throw away the defective product or packaging
Do not accept a partial refund if you are owed more
Do not miss hearing dates

rights.right: To a refund, replacement, repair or compensation
To refuse unfair contract terms and misleading advertisements
To file a complaint where you live, not only where the seller is
To file without a lawyer and online
Medical services for a fee are covered
rights.source: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha

rights.right: Homebuyers can get a refund for inordinate delay in possession
rights.source: Pioneer Urban Land v. Govindan Raghavan

documents: Photos or videos of the defect
Copy of legal notice and postal receipt

title: Online fraud, UPI scam or hacked account
summary: If money was taken through a fraudulent call, link, UPI request or a hacked account, speed matters. Reporting within hours improves the chance of freezing the money.
urgent: Call 1930 immediately. The first few hours (the 'golden hour') are the best chance of blocking the money.

steps.title: Call 1930 right away
steps.detail: Report the fraud on the National Cyber Crime Helpline 1930 or at cybercrime.gov.in. Give the transaction ID, amount, time and the fraudster's account or UPI ID.
steps.why: The helpline can alert banks to freeze the money in the recipient account.

steps.title: Inform your bank and block your cards and UPI
steps.detail: Call your bank's customer care, block your card, UPI and net banking, and file a written complaint. Note the complaint reference number.
steps.why: Reporting within 3 working days can give you zero liability under RBI rules.

steps.title: Secure your accounts
steps.detail: Change passwords and PINs, log out of all devices, enable two-factor authentication, and uninstall any screen-sharing or remote-access app you were asked to install.
steps.why: This prevents further losses.

steps.title: Preserve evidence
steps.detail: Take screenshots of messages, call logs, the fraud website or link, the transaction SMS and the bank statement. Do not delete anything.
steps.why: Needed for the police complaint and the bank claim.

steps.title: File a police complaint or FIR
steps.detail: Complete the complaint on cybercrime.gov.in or file at your local cyber cell or police station under the IT Act and BNS (cheating by personation, identity theft).
steps.why: IT Act Sections 66C and 66D; BNS Sections 318 and 319.

steps.title: Escalate with the bank, then the RBI Ombudsman
steps.detail: If the bank does not reverse the amount or reply within 30 days, file a complaint at cms.rbi.org.in.
steps.why: RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021.

steps.title: For hacked social media or morphed images
steps.detail: Report the account or post to the platform's Grievance Officer. Platforms must remove intimate or morphed images within 24 hours of your complaint.
steps.why: IT Rules, 2021.

dos: Act within minutes or hours
Keep the transaction IDs and complaint numbers
Tell your family about common scams
donts: Never share an OTP, PIN or CVV with anyone, including 'bank officials' or 'police'
Do not approve unknown UPI 'collect' requests; you never need to enter a PIN to receive money
Do not pay 'recovery agents' who promise to get your money back
There is no such thing as a 'digital arrest'; real police do not ask for money on video calls

rights.right: Zero liability if reported within 3 working days for third-party fraud
Bank must credit the disputed amount (shadow reversal) within 10 working days
Free complaint to the RBI Ombudsman
Identity theft and online cheating are criminal offences
Platforms must remove non-consensual intimate images within 24 hours

documents: Bank statement showing the fraudulent debit
Screenshots of messages, links, call logs
Acknowledgement number from 1930 or the cyber portal

authorities.name: RBI Ombudsman
authorities.role: If the bank does not resolve within 30 days

portals.name: Sanchar Saathi (report fraud calls, block lost phones)

title: Cheque bounced or money not returned
summary: A bounced cheque is a criminal offence if you follow the strict timelines. For money lent without a cheque, a legal notice and a recovery suit are the usual route.
urgent: Deadlines are strict: send the notice within 30 days of the bank's return memo.

steps.title: Collect the return memo
steps.detail: Get the cheque return memo from your bank stating the reason (for example 'funds insufficient'). Keep the original cheque.
steps.why: The memo starts the 30-day clock for the notice.

steps.title: Send a demand notice within 30 days
steps.detail: Send a written legal notice to the drawer by registered post (and email or WhatsApp if possible) demanding payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of receiving the notice.
steps.why: NI Act Section 138(b).

steps.title: Wait 15 days from delivery of the notice
steps.detail: Track the postal delivery. If the drawer pays, the matter ends.
steps.why: The offence is complete only if payment is not made within 15 days.

steps.title: File a complaint within one month
steps.detail: File a complaint before the Magistrate's court in the area of your bank branch within 30 days after the 15-day period ends.
steps.why: NI Act Section 142.

steps.title: Ask for interim compensation
steps.detail: Request the court to order interim compensation of up to 20% of the cheque amount.
steps.why: NI Act Section 143A.

steps.title: Consider settlement
steps.detail: The case can be settled at any stage, including in Lok Adalat or mediation.
steps.why: NI Act Section 147; Kanchan Mehta.

steps.title: If there was no cheque
steps.detail: For money lent without a cheque, send a legal notice and then file a civil recovery suit (a summary suit if there is a written acknowledgement) within three years.
steps.why: Code of Civil Procedure Order XXXVII; Limitation Act.

dos: Keep the original cheque and return memo safely
Keep postal receipts and tracking printouts
Calculate all deadlines carefully
donts: Do not miss the 30-day notice window
Do not present the cheque after its 3-month validity
Do not accept a fresh post-dated cheque without written terms

rights.right: Criminal complaint for dishonour of cheque
To file in the court where your bank branch is
Interim compensation up to 20%
Fine up to twice the cheque amount

documents: Proof of the debt (agreement, messages, bank transfers)

title: Landlord or tenant dispute
summary: Problems with eviction, the security deposit, rent increases or cutting of water or electricity. A landlord cannot evict you by force; due process is required.
urgent: If you are being forcibly thrown out or locked out, call 112; forcible dispossession and trespass are offences.

steps.title: Read your rent agreement
steps.detail: Check the notice period, deposit terms, lock-in period, and rent increase clauses. Also check whether your State has a rent control or tenancy law.
steps.why: The agreement and State law decide most rights.

steps.title: Communicate in writing
steps.detail: Raise the issue with the landlord or tenant by email or message and keep records. Pay rent through a bank or UPI so there is proof.
steps.why: Written records are your evidence.

steps.title: Document the property condition
steps.detail: Take dated photos and videos when moving in and out, and get the keys handed over in writing.
steps.why: This prevents unfair deductions from the deposit.

steps.title: Send a legal notice
steps.detail: For a withheld deposit or illegal actions, send a legal notice demanding the refund or compliance within 15 days.
steps.why: This is often enough to resolve the dispute.

steps.title: Approach the Rent Authority or Civil Court
steps.detail: Depending on your State, approach the Rent Controller or Rent Authority, or file a civil suit for recovery of the deposit or for an injunction.
steps.why: The Transfer of Property Act and State rent laws provide the remedies.

steps.title: If dispossessed illegally
steps.detail: File a police complaint for trespass or criminal intimidation, and a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act within 6 months to recover possession.
steps.why: Even the owner cannot forcibly evict a person in settled possession (Rame Gowda).

dos: Get a registered or notarised rent agreement
Keep rent receipts
Give and ask for proper written notice
donts: Landlords: do not cut off water or electricity or change locks to force eviction
Tenants: do not stop paying rent during a dispute; deposit it in a way you can prove
Do not leave belongings behind without an inventory

rights.right: No eviction without due process of law
rights.source: Specific Relief Act Section 6; Rame Gowda v. M. Varadappa Naidu

rights.right: Written notice before termination of tenancy (15 days for monthly tenancies, unless agreed otherwise)
Refund of the security deposit on vacating, after lawful deductions
rights.source: Rent agreement; Model Tenancy Act Section 11 where adopted

rights.right: Essential services cannot be cut off
rights.source: Model Tenancy Act Section 20 where adopted; State rent laws

rights.right: Landlord's entry with prior notice
rights.source: Model Tenancy Act Section 17 where adopted

title: Road accident
summary: Whether you were injured, lost a family member, or want to help a victim, here is what to do and how to claim compensation.
urgent: Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance. Hospitals must give emergency treatment without waiting for police formalities.

steps.title: Get medical help immediately
steps.detail: Call 108 or 112. Any hospital must give emergency care. Cashless treatment of up to Rs. 1.5 lakh for 7 days is available under the government scheme at designated hospitals.
steps.why: Parmanand Katara v. Union of India; MV Act Section 162.

steps.title: Note the details
steps.detail: Note the vehicle number, make and colour, the time and place, and the names and phone numbers of witnesses. Take photos of the scene and vehicles.
steps.why: Needed for the FIR and the compensation claim.

steps.title: Make sure an FIR is registered
steps.detail: The police will register an FIR and prepare a Detailed Accident Report (DAR). Get a copy of the FIR.
steps.why: The DAR is treated as a claim application before the tribunal.

steps.title: Keep medical and expense records
steps.detail: Keep all hospital bills, prescriptions, discharge summaries, disability certificates, and proof of income lost.
steps.why: Compensation is calculated from these.

steps.title: File a claim before the MACT
steps.detail: File a claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal where the accident happened or where you live, within six months. Compensation covers medical costs, loss of income, pain and suffering, and, in death cases, loss of dependency.
steps.why: MV Act Section 166; Sarla Verma and Pranay Sethi on computation.

steps.title: For hit-and-run cases
steps.detail: If the vehicle cannot be traced, apply to the Claims Enquiry Officer (SDM or Tehsildar) for fixed compensation: Rs. 2 lakh for death, Rs. 50,000 for grievous hurt.
steps.why: MV Act Section 161.

dos: Help victims; Good Samaritans are protected by law
Keep the insurance details of the vehicles involved
Get a lawyer or DLSA help for the claim
donts: Do not move the vehicles before photos unless needed for safety
Do not sign a settlement with the insurer without understanding the full claim
Do not leave the scene if you were driving; inform the police within 24 hours

rights.right: To emergency treatment without police formalities
rights.source: Parmanand Katara v. Union of India

rights.right: Good Samaritans cannot be harassed or forced to give their identity
Compensation of Rs. 5 lakh (death) or Rs. 2.5 lakh (grievous hurt) without proving fault
Hit-and-run compensation
Full compensation through the MACT

documents: Death certificate and post-mortem report (fatal cases)

title: Elderly parent neglected or property taken
summary: Senior citizens and parents can claim maintenance from their children and can even cancel a property transfer if the children stop caring for them.
urgent: Elder Line 14567 provides help, information and rescue for senior citizens.

steps.title: Call Elder Line 14567
steps.detail: The national helpline for senior citizens gives information, emotional support and help with abuse cases.
steps.why: Immediate support and guidance.

steps.title: Apply to the Maintenance Tribunal
steps.detail: File a simple application before the Maintenance Tribunal (usually the SDM's office) against your children, grandchildren or heirs. No lawyer is needed.
steps.why: Senior Citizens Act Sections 4 and 5.

steps.title: Ask for interim maintenance
steps.detail: The Tribunal can order interim maintenance while the case is pending and should decide within 90 days.
steps.why: Senior Citizens Act Section 5.

steps.title: Challenge a property transfer
steps.detail: If you gifted or transferred property to a child on the understanding that they would care for you and they did not, ask the Tribunal to declare the transfer void.
steps.why: Senior Citizens Act Section 23.

steps.title: Report abuse or abandonment
steps.detail: Physical abuse, threats or abandonment can be reported to the police.
steps.why: Senior Citizens Act Section 24 and BNS.

dos: Keep documents of your property and income in a safe place
Tell a trusted friend or neighbour about any abuse
Ask the Tribunal for a Maintenance Officer's help
donts: Do not sign property papers under pressure
Do not hand over bank passwords or cheque books

rights.right: To maintenance from children and heirs
A simple, quick procedure without a lawyer
To cancel a property transfer if care is not provided
Abandonment of a senior citizen is an offence
Parents can also claim maintenance under criminal law

documents: Details of children and their income
Property documents and any gift deed

title: Child abuse, child labour or child marriage
summary: Any person who knows of sexual abuse of a child must report it. Child labour and child marriage can also be stopped by the authorities.
urgent: Call the Child Helpline 1098 or 112. Ensure the child is safe first.

steps.title: Ensure the child is safe
steps.detail: Remove the child from the abuser's reach and keep them with a trusted adult. Do not confront the abuser in front of the child.
steps.why: The child's safety and wellbeing come first.

steps.title: Report to 1098, the police or the Special Juvenile Police Unit
steps.detail: Report sexual abuse to the police or SJPU. Reporting is mandatory under POCSO, and anyone reporting in good faith is protected.
steps.why: POCSO Sections 19 and 21.

steps.title: Get medical care
steps.detail: Take the child for medical examination at a government hospital, preferably by a woman doctor for a girl child, in the presence of a parent or trusted person.
steps.why: Medical examination is evidence and the child needs care.

steps.title: Child-friendly statement
steps.detail: The child's statement should be recorded at home or a place of their choice by a woman officer not in uniform. The child's identity must be kept confidential.
steps.why: POCSO Sections 23 and 24.

steps.title: Approach the Child Welfare Committee
steps.detail: For care, counselling, shelter or rehabilitation, the child can be produced before the Child Welfare Committee (CWC).
steps.why: Juvenile Justice Act.

steps.title: Child labour or child marriage
steps.detail: Report child labour to 1098, the police or the Labour Department, and an intended child marriage to the Child Marriage Prohibition Officer, the police or the Magistrate, who can stop it.
steps.why: Child Labour Act; Prohibition of Child Marriage Act.

dos: Believe and reassure the child
Write down what the child said in their own words
Seek counselling support
donts: Do not blame or repeatedly question the child
Do not share the child's identity on social media
Do not try to settle the matter privately

rights.right: Mandatory reporting of sexual offences against children
Child-friendly statement recording and trial
Identity of the child must not be disclosed
Free and compulsory education; no corporal punishment
No child below 14 may be employed
rights.source: Child and Adolescent Labour Act Section 3

documents: Notes of what the child disclosed
Any messages, photos or other evidence

portals.name: National Cyber Crime Portal (child abuse material)

title: Getting information from a government office
summary: Use the Right to Information Act to find the status of your file, application, pension, scholarship or complaint, or to get copies of government records.

steps.title: Identify the public authority
steps.detail: Find the department or office that holds the information and its Public Information Officer (PIO).
steps.why: The application goes to the PIO of that authority.

steps.title: Write clear questions
steps.detail: Ask for specific information or documents (for example: the daily progress report of my application dated ..., copies of file notings). No reason needs to be given.
steps.why: RTI Act Section 6(2).

steps.title: Pay the fee and submit
steps.detail: Pay Rs. 10 for central authorities (State fees vary) and file online at rtionline.gov.in or by post. Applicants below the poverty line pay no fee.
steps.why: RTI Act Section 6.

steps.title: Wait 30 days
steps.detail: The PIO must reply within 30 days, or 48 hours if the matter concerns life or liberty.
steps.why: RTI Act Section 7.

steps.title: File a first appeal
steps.detail: If there is no reply or the reply is incomplete, file a first appeal within 30 days to the First Appellate Authority.
steps.why: RTI Act Section 19(1).

steps.title: File a second appeal or complaint
steps.detail: If still unsatisfied, file a second appeal within 90 days with the Central or State Information Commission, which can also penalise the PIO.
steps.why: RTI Act Sections 19(3) and 20.

dos: Keep questions short and specific
Keep the receipt or registration number
Track deadlines from the date of receipt
donts: Do not ask 'why' questions or for opinions; ask for records
Do not combine unrelated subjects in one application

rights.right: Access to information held by public authorities
No need to give reasons
Reply within 30 days, or 48 hours for life and liberty
Free information if the reply is late
Penalty on a PIO for delay or refusal

title: Caste-based abuse or discrimination
summary: Insults, threats, violence, boycott or land grabbing targeting members of Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes are serious offences with special protections for victims.
urgent: If you are in danger, call 112.

steps.title: File an FIR under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act
steps.detail: Go to the police station and file an FIR. No preliminary enquiry is needed before registration.
steps.why: SC/ST Act Section 18A.

steps.title: Escalate if the FIR is refused
steps.detail: Complain to the SP, the District Magistrate, or the State or National Commission for Scheduled Castes or Tribes. Wilful neglect of duty by a public servant is itself an offence.
steps.why: SC/ST Act Section 4.

steps.title: Claim relief and protection
steps.detail: Victims are entitled to monetary relief, travel and maintenance expenses during investigation and trial, and protection.
steps.why: SC/ST Act Section 15A and the Rules.

steps.title: Get free legal aid
steps.detail: Members of SC/ST communities are entitled to free legal services. Contact the DLSA.
steps.why: Legal Services Authorities Act Section 12(a).

dos: Note the exact words used and witnesses present
Record videos where safe
Get medical treatment and a report for any injury
donts: Do not accept pressure to compromise
Do not miss court dates; you have a right to be informed of them

rights.right: FIR without preliminary enquiry
rights.source: SC/ST Act Section 18A; Prathvi Raj Chauhan

rights.right: No anticipatory bail for the accused where a prima facie case exists
Relief, rehabilitation and protection
Trial in Special Courts
Untouchability is abolished

authorities.name: National / State Commission for Scheduled Castes or Tribes
